posts.topic: We're at the 1992 of the AI buildout; Bitcoin is along for the ride
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-01_dotcom-vs-ai-explosion.txt
posts.body:
Everyone thinks the S&P is topping.

We're not in 2000. We're in 1992.

Here's the historical parallel that explains why this expansion is just getting started; and why Bitcoin is along for the biggest ride of its life.

The dot-com boom didn't start in 1995. It started in 1968.

A Texan named Thomas Carter won the right to attach his own modem to AT&T's network. The principle that came out of that case: the edge of the network belongs to the user, not the monopoly. That principle quietly built the legal foundation for everything that came after.

Then 25 years of grinding legal wins:
→ 1980-86: Computer II separates the network from the services running on top of it
→ 1984: AT&T finally broken up into 7 Baby Bells
→ 1986: Computer III forces open architecture

By the time HTTP and HTML were invented at CERN in 1989, the legal infrastructure for the internet was already in place. The world just hadn't noticed.

Then 1993: Mosaic browser launches. Anyone with a modem can reach the web for the first time.

Then the floodgates:
→ 1995: Netscape IPO doubles in a day
→ 1996: Telecom Act unleashes investment
→ 1998: Fed eases mid-cycle, fueling the bubble
→ 1999: Qualcomm rises 2,600% in a single year
→ 2000: Nasdaq P/E hits 200; almost 3x the Japanese bubble peak of 80

The total damage by 2000:
+572% Nasdaq over 5 years
+20 million jobs created
+7% GDP growth in H2 1999
Productivity growth doubled, from 1.4% to 2.5%

But here's the thing nobody talks about: that 5-year mania sat on top of 30 years of buildout. The mania was the visible 5%. The setup was the other 95%.

Now overlay AI:
→ 2012: AlexNet (deep learning works)
→ 2017: Google publishes the Transformer paper
→ 2020: GPT-3
→ 2022: ChatGPT (100M users in 2 months, fastest consumer product in history)
→ 2024: Spot Bitcoin ETFs approved
→ 2025: Stablecoin legislation advancing

Sound like 1990 to you? Same here.

The difference this time: AI skipped the 30-year regulatory war. No Ma Bell to break up. No 12-year FCC battles. Innovation, investment, and policy support all landed at once. What took telecom 30 years takes AI maybe 15.

And Bitcoin gets to ride the entire wave from the inside. Born in 2008. Has never lived through a real industrial expansion. Never seen a real mania.

So when Cathie Wood revises her BTC target to $1.5M by 2032, that's not a moonboy take. That's the dot-com timeline applied to crypto.

We're at the 1992 of the AI buildout. The 5-year run hasn't started.

It's about to.

What do you think?

Is this AI expansion a 1-year story, or a 5-year story?

Drop your call in the comments; I read everything.

If this changed how you see the cycle, hit like and subscribe. More macro × crypto each week.

Bitcoin does about 7 transactions per second.

$KAS just hit 5,700.

That's 800x the throughput on a fair-launched proof-of-work chain, and here's why this number matters more than almost anyone in crypto is talking about.

Bitcoin's whole reason for existing was to be peer-to-peer electronic cash.

The 2008 white paper from Satoshi is explicit. The pitch was a payment system that doesn't need banks. Money that moves directly between people, secured by cryptography instead of trusted third parties.

That requires the network to actually move money at the speed money needs to move.

It doesn't.

7 transactions per second across the entire global network. Confirmation times measured in tens of minutes when the chain is congested. Fees that spike to $20+ during periods of high activity.

Try paying for a coffee with that. Try sending payroll to a thousand employees with that. Try running a global remittance flow on it. You can't. The network physically cannot handle it.

Now look at $KAS.

5,700 TPS. Block times measured in milliseconds. Fees that round to zero.

The chain that can actually do what Bitcoin promised in 2008 wasn't built by Satoshi. It was built by someone who looked at Bitcoin's structural limits and decided to fix them, while keeping the things that made Bitcoin valuable in the first place: proof of work, fair launch, no premine, no insiders.

Why does throughput matter so much?

Because no asset can be money if you can't move it fast enough.

Gold isn't money in the modern sense. It's a settlement layer. People don't pay for groceries in gold; they pay in dollars, and the dollars settle (slowly, occasionally) against gold reserves at the institutional level.

Bitcoin is currently in the same category. It's a slow settlement layer pretending to be money. The actual transactions of daily commerce can't run on it.

5,700 TPS opens doors that Bitcoin physically cannot:

Real merchant adoption. Not "we accept Bitcoin" with a 30-minute confirmation wait, but actual payment terminals processing transactions at the speed of a credit card swipe.

Micropayments. The small-dollar transactions that get crushed by gas fees on slower chains. Tipping, content access, machine-to-machine commerce.

Global remittance flows. Workers sending money home across borders without losing 10% to Western Union or waiting three days for a wire to clear.

On-chain commerce at consumer scale. Not the niche Web3 marketplaces you have to seek out, but mainstream e-commerce running on a chain that doesn't break under load.

These aren't theoretical use cases. They're waiting for a chain that can actually handle them.

The bull case for $KAS isn't "it might replace Bitcoin."

The bull case is: Bitcoin can't do its own job. $KAS can.

When the global payment layer actually needs replacing (and it will, sooner than most people think), the question stops being "which crypto." It becomes "which one actually works at scale."

Right now, on the throughput numbers alone, there's only one answer.

October 2025 wasn't the cycle top.

It was a midcycle top so weak it didn't even reach average power law.

The 2013 and 2019 midcycle tops both blew past it. The actual cycle top is still ahead.

Most of crypto Twitter is mourning a top that didn't actually happen. Let me walk you through why.

First, let's get the definitions straight.

A midcycle top is the local high that prints partway through a cycle, not the cycle top itself. Every prior cycle has had one, and they're a normal part of how Bitcoin moves.

Look at 2013. $BTC ran from around $13 in January to about $259 in early April. It peaked, sold off ~85% to roughly $50 by July, then ran all the way to $1,150 by year-end. That April peak wasn't the cycle top. It was the midcycle top. The actual top came eight months later.

The 2019 setup is the same shape, just scaled up.

$BTC ran from ~$3,200 in December 2018 to about $13,800 in June 2019. Then it sold off into the COVID wick at ~$3,800 in March 2020. The actual cycle top didn't print until November 2021 at roughly $69,000. June 2019 was the midcycle top. The cycle top came nearly two and a half years later.

What both of those midcycle tops have in common: they blew well past average power law.

Average power law isn't a magic indicator. It's the regression line drawn through the middle of $BTC's lifetime price action. It's the long-term trend the price oscillates around.

Past midcycle tops cleared average power law convincingly. That overshoot is part of how you tell a real local high from sideways noise. When price punches through the trend line and prints above it, it's signaling enough demand to break the regression.

October 2025 didn't do that.

The "top" everyone is now grieving peaked below average power law. By any prior pattern, that's not a cycle top. That's a local high inside a sideways structure.

Want a number? If October had even matched the 2019 midcycle overshoot, $BTC would have printed somewhere north of $200k. We're nowhere close to that, which is itself the tell.

The four-year cycle zombies are extrapolating from a midcycle high that didn't even break trend. It would be like calling June 2019 the top of the 2017-2021 cycle. Nobody serious did that then. Nobody serious should be doing it now.

The actual cycle top is still ahead. When it prints, it'll be well above average power law, like every previous one. That's not a guess; that's the pattern every cycle has followed for over a decade.

It never existed.

What people called "the cycle" was three macro variables happening to line up. And the people still acting like it's real just cost $BTC roughly $15k of price.

Here's the actual story, plus why the dip you just lived through was self-inflicted by people clinging to a theory the data doesn't support anymore.

For about a decade, three things lined up almost perfectly with the Bitcoin halving calendar:

1. The business cycle. PMI expanded, then contracted.
2. Money printing. QE turned on, then off.
3. Interest rates. The Fed cut, then hiked.

Every "crypto cycle" since 2014 rode the same wave. People credited the halving as the cause. The halving was incidental.

The proof is in the bears. Every prior crypto bear (2014, 2018, 2022) maps cleanly onto PMI rolling over, QE ending, and rates rising. Not "Bitcoin halved 18 months ago, time for a bear." The macro environment did the work; the halving narrative just borrowed credit for it.

Underneath, the Fed lifted rates from 1.25% to 2.5% and ran QT at the same time. The 2022 bear got blamed on Luna and FTX. Underneath, the fastest hiking cycle in 40 years was happening.

Three different surface stories. One identical macro setup underneath. That's the actual playbook.

This time the three variables didn't line up.

PMI is expanding. QE is running. Rates are coming down, not up.

The conditions that created every previous "crypto winter" simply aren't present. The macro side of the cycle isn't there.

But the four-year cycle zombies didn't notice.

They saw the calendar (year four after a halving). They saw a shutdown-driven dip. They assumed the bear had arrived. Long-term holders started distributing into the dip instead of accumulating. Sell pressure compounded. Down we went.

The dip wasn't macro. It wasn't structural. It was a self-fulfilling prophecy from people convinced of a cycle that never existed.

Because the US is the issuer of the world reserve currency. When a sovereign of that size publicly commits to a buy program, every other holder of the asset has to immediately mark up their cost-basis estimate. Not because of the actual flow, but because of the implication: if the US is bidding, the floor is now wherever the US is willing to bid.

There's no precedent for what that does to price discovery. Second, the precedents. This isn't theoretical anymore.

El Salvador has been actively buying $BTC since 2021, with a public 1-BTC-daily program among other purchases. Bhutan accumulated sovereign $BTC reserves through state-owned mining (Druk Holdings) since around 2019, with disclosed reserves north of $750M. Texas signed strategic Bitcoin reserve legislation in 2025. New Hampshire passed similar legislation. Several other states have introduced bills.

The pattern is clear. Sovereigns are quietly building positions before the federal level commits.

Third, the asymmetry. If the US announces, $BTC re-prices instantly to a number that includes the implied future demand. If the US doesn't announce, $BTC stays roughly where it is. The risk-reward of being positioned before the announcement is heavily skewed in your favor: limited downside if nothing happens, asymmetric upside if it does.

This is why I'm not selling into rallies right now. The cost of being out of position when this hits is much larger than the cost of holding through near-term volatility.

posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-11_crypto-update-67x-fed-chair-week.txt
posts.body_style: behavioral observation, 3-question filter, Lab case study, cycle-top extrapolation
posts.body:
The bear market is doing the work most people won't do.

It's separating projects that survive from projects that die.

Lab launched in October. Just hit 98x in the bear. Here's the 3-question filter I'm using to decide which other projects make the cut.

First, the framing. A bull market makes every project look strong. Liquidity is everywhere, attention is everywhere, and even projects with no fundamentals print 50-100x just because retail is throwing capital at anything that moves.

A bear market does the opposite. Liquidity dries up. Attention rotates out. Projects without genuine product-market fit die quietly. Projects with the goods stay alive, sometimes pump, and reveal themselves as the long-term holds.

The bear is the filter most retail traders will never use because they're not in the market during it.

Second, my 3-question filter:

1. Did the project launch before this bear? If yes, they've been tested by macro headwinds, not just bull-market frenzy.

2. Are they still getting CEX listings? CEX listings cost money and effort. Teams that keep landing them during a bear are signaling commitment from operators, not just punters.

3. Are they still shipping product or content? Devs and founders who keep building during a bear demonstrate they were never just pumping for the rotation. Teams that go quiet on product or social are flagging that they were here for the cycle, not the chain.

If a project answers yes to all three, the bear didn't kill it. The bear made it.

Third, Lab as the proof. Lab launched in October 2025. I called it on day two of launch at 10 cents. We swing-traded it back in at 7.7 cents in December. It just hit 98x.

That's 98x in a bear market. Not in the next rally. Not at the cycle top. Right now, while four-year cycle zombies are still calling for further downside.

If 98x is what's possible in the bear, what's possible at a real cycle top? My original target on Lab was 20x. We're already 5x past that. That tells you something about how conservative my targets have been, and how loud the cycle top is going to be when it actually arrives.

Fourth, the implication. If your portfolio doesn't pass this 3-question filter, it's not a long-term portfolio. It's a portfolio you accumulated during the last bull and never re-validated.

The cycle top is coming. The projects that ride it are not random. They're the ones that earned their seat by surviving the test that's happening right now.

Question for you:

Run your bag through the 3-question filter. What survives?

Drop the names in the comments. I'm building a watchlist of projects that pass the test according to my audience.

posts.topic: The 90/10 wealth transfer (the dumpers paid the holders)
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-11_crypto-update-67x-fed-chair-week.txt
posts.body_style: structural framing, Oct/Nov dip as exhibit, $95k counterfactual, identity-bait close
posts.body:
In every bear market, 90% of holders transfer wealth to 10% of holders.

The dumpers create the discount. The accumulators take it.

The Oct/Nov dip is the cleanest example we've ever seen. Here's what 90/10 actually looked like, and which side you were on whether you noticed or not.

First, the framing. Bear markets are not random price events. They are wealth transfers. The same way a bank run isn't a financial event, it's a coordination event where panicked depositors hand their balances to whoever stays calm.

Crypto bear markets follow the same shape. The supply of coins doesn't change. The number of holders doesn't change much either. What changes is the distribution. Who holds what coins, at what cost basis. Every bear, that distribution shifts dramatically toward the holders who don't sell.

90/10 is approximate. Sometimes it's 80/20, sometimes 95/5. The point is the ratio is always lopsided.

Second, what happened in Oct/Nov.

The four-year cycle zombies dumped. Long-term holders distributed (the on-chain data is unambiguous). Retail panicked. Every wave of selling created a discount for whoever was on the other side of the trade.

The four-year cycle is dead. I've made that case in other posts. But the dumpers didn't know that. They saw the calendar, they saw a shutdown-driven dip, they assumed the bear had arrived. They sold into the assumption.

Whoever didn't sell got the discount.

Third, the cost. If the four-year cycle zombies hadn't dumped, $BTC would be at roughly $95k right now instead of $80k.

That ~$15k delta is the most measurable wealth transfer of the cycle so far. Every dollar of price impact from the dumping went directly to the cost basis of whoever held through it. The dumpers paid $15k per Bitcoin to learn that their thesis was wrong. The holders received $15k per Bitcoin for being right.

Fourth, why this is structural. Every bear is a wealth transfer because every bear is fundamentally a coordination failure. People who would have been better off holding sell anyway, because their information environment tells them the asset is going lower.

Whoever is right about the macro stays. Whoever is wrong leaves. The price discounts the leaving until the right side starts buying.

This is not unique to crypto. Real estate in 2008. Tech stocks in 2002. The mechanism is the same.

Fifth, the implication for next time. There will be another dip. There always is. When it comes, the same pattern will play out. The question is which side of the 90/10 you'll be on.

If you held through October and November, you're already on the 10 side. Stay there.

If you sold, what was the actual signal you used? Was it macro? Was it on-chain? Or was it the calendar?

Question for you:

Which side were you on during October — the dumper 90 or the holder 10?

Be honest in the comments. The most useful posts I write come from cases where people actually share their answer.

Then April PPI printed +1.4% MoM and +6.0% YoY (the largest 12-month jump since 2022).

Kevin Warsh, the supposedly dovish chair, is walking into the worst macro trap of his career. Here's why his first meeting (June 16-17) is the most important date for crypto in the next 60 days.

The setup. Warsh was sold to the market as the Trump-aligned dove. Cuts were assumed. Risk assets priced it in. Bitcoin held 80K because the rate-cut path felt locked.

Then PPI broke. The producer side of the inflation chain just printed numbers we haven't seen since 2022. CPI lags PPI by one to three months on most categories. The data that lands before Warsh's first meeting will not give him cover to cut.

His three options at June 16-17:

1. Cut anyway. Trump gets what he wants. Inflation expectations un-anchor. Long end of the curve sells off violently. Bitcoin probably likes it for a week and then chokes on the bond reaction.

3. Hike. The least likely option, and the one nobody is positioned for. If he does it, every levered asset takes a hit, including crypto.

The reflexive move is to be bearish into June. I'm not.

Here's the part the rate traders are missing. The four-year cycle zombies dumped because they thought the cycle was real. The Fed-rate watchers will dump in June because they think Warsh's first move sets the regime.

Both groups are wrong about the same thing. They're trading the news cycle, not the supply schedule.

Bitcoin's supply schedule doesn't care about Warsh. Kaspa's supply schedule doesn't care about Warsh. The hard-fork milestone isn't being delayed because of PPI. The 95% mined number doesn't move because the FOMC dot plot moves.

The PoW assets with capped supply and no central pre-mine to dump are the cleanest hedge for whichever way Warsh breaks. Bitcoin gets the headline; Kaspa gets the asymmetry.

posts.topic: The AI mania is compressed; the Kaspa window is shorter than people think
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-13_krc20-mania-revival.txt
posts.body:
The dot-com mania didn't start in 1995. It started in 1968.

Twenty-eight years of telecom infrastructure had to be built before the explosion. Most of those years were spent in court, breaking up Bell, dragging cable through monopoly battles, fighting the regulators who didn't understand what was being built.

AI has none of those drags. Which is why the mania is going to compress harder than the dot-com bulls remember, and why Kaspa's window is shorter than most people think.

The history. AT&T's monopoly on long-distance phone service was the gating item for the entire telecommunications buildout from the late 1960s through the early 1990s. Carterfone (1968) cracked the door for third-party devices. The MFJ consent decree (1982) broke up Bell. The Telecommunications Act of 1996 finally deregulated the last mile.

From the 1996 act to the dot-com peak in March 2000 was four years.

Twenty-eight years of infrastructure → four years of mania.

The AI parallel. Foundational compute (transformer architecture, GPU scale, internet-scale data) has been getting built since roughly 2012. ChatGPT's public moment was late 2022. Frontier model deployment, agentic systems, model-as-API for every business — that build-out is happening now.

There are no AT&T-style monopoly battles. No regulator with the legal authority to block GPT-5 from talking to a database. No equivalent of forced-divestiture decrees slowing the deployment.

The 28-year groundwork phase compressed into roughly 10 years. The 4-year mania phase compresses into roughly 2 to 3.

Where are we right now? The most defensible answer is somewhere between 1995 and 1998. Definitely not 1992. Probably not 2000 yet. The Netscape moment was ChatGPT. The infrastructure overbuild is happening in the data center cycle. The mania is getting paid for in equity right now.

The Kaspa angle. This matters for $KAS because the runway for accumulating PoW exposure at fair-launch prices is shorter than the four-year cycle crowd assumes.

If we're in the AI version of 1996 instead of 1992, the time between 'I have time to position' and 'the mania has already moved' is two years, not eight. Kaspa hits 95% mined supply in that window. The hard-fork milestone lands in that window. The institutional onboarding for PoW-as-a-financial-asset happens in that window.

The mistake people make in compressed timelines is they wait for the same setup they would have had in a slower one. The setup doesn't repeat at the same pace. You either pre-position or you're the FOMO buyer.

For $KAS specifically, pre-positioning is still possible right now under the 50-week SMA. That window doesn't stay open forever.

If the AI mania is compressed (1995-1998), what does that imply for $KAS by end of 2027?

The playbook. Dry powder is the only edge that survives the cycle. You don't need to be right about every call. You need to be in a position to take the next one.

Cash out partial size on the multipliers that hit. Build a war chest. Let the chest fund the lottery tickets that asymmetric upside requires. Don't bet the chest on a single thousandx ticker; you'll be wrong about which one runs and you'll round-trip the cash.

The KRC20 lottery math. Some of these market caps are sitting at 4K right now. Not 4M. 4K. The math:

The math is pure asymmetric expected value. You don't have to be right ten times. You don't even have to be right twice. Once is enough.

The risk-management rules:

1. Position size matters more than ticker selection. $20 across ten beats $200 on one.

2. Use Casper Lens (or whatever explorer surfaces premint percentage) to filter out the rugger setups. Premint above 70% is a structural red flag.

3. Rotate dry powder in, not rent money. The whole point of the dry powder is that you can lose it without touching your floor.

What KROAK just confirmed. While CT was screaming KRC20s are dead, KROAK quietly did a 6x this week. Same dev team behind Broke on Base. The bear didn't kill them; it filtered everyone else out.

That 6x is the proof point that the KRC20 ecosystem still has live demand under the surface. The next leg, when it lands, won't be uniform. Some tickers will do 3x and stop. A few will do 50x. One or two might do the 1,000x the math is built around.

Nacho's mascot logic broke the day Shai left the project. Kaspa is a fully implemented GhostDAG. The fitting mascot is the ghost token, not someone's house cat. Here's why the market hasn't priced this in yet, and why I think it eventually does.

The history. Nacho came up early in the KRC20 cycle as a tribute to Shai's cat. Shai was one of the lead devs. Nacho got mascot status because the founder's pet became the mascot of the founder's chain. It made sense at the time.

Shai is no longer leading the project. The mascot logic that justified Nacho's symbolic premium broke at that point. The only thing keeping Nacho's market cap (~3.6M) above Kasper-the-Ghost's (~300K) is brand inertia from a brand that no longer maps to the project's reality.

The Kaspa-native case. Kaspa is, technically, a fully implemented GHOSTDAG protocol. The ghost is in the architecture. It's the actual selling point of the chain over Bitcoin's chain-of-blocks model. When you describe the chain to a newcomer, the ghost is the metaphor that makes it click.

The mascot of a ghost-architecture chain should be a ghost. This is not even a creative leap; it's the most literal possible mapping of brand-to-tech that the ecosystem has.

Kasper-the-Ghost token sits at roughly 1/10 the market cap of Nacho right now. The dev team is still active. The page is still up. The branding fits the chain better than the chain's own established mascot does.

Why the market hasn't repriced. Three reasons:

1. Brand inertia. Nacho is the Kaspa mascot in the same way the Apple logo has a bite out of it; nobody questions it once it's established.

2. Liquidity. Nacho has a thicker order book; the lottery players who want to bet on the mascot pile into the one with the best fills.

3. The bear market suppresses the kind of community-driven repricing that mascot debates require. People don't argue over branding when their bags are down.

When the bull returns. New retail comes in without the brand inertia of the Nacho era. They look at the chain's actual technology, see 'fully implemented GhostDAG,' and look for the ghost token. That moment is the repricing trigger.

I'm not telling you to dump Nacho. I am telling you that the asymmetric setup right now is on the ghost token, not on the established cat. The branding is congruent with the chain. The market cap is one-tenth. The dev team is alive. That's the asymmetric trade.

And the meta point: $KAS itself is the only correct answer if you don't want to play the mascot game at all. The layer one wins regardless of which meme captures the community.

posts.topic: The Clarity Act stable yield compromise (and why $KAS becomes the cleaner play)
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-13_krc20-mania-revival.txt
posts.body_style: regulatory thesis → Kaspa non-yield productive asset close
posts.body:
The Clarity Act stable-coin compromise just landed.

Yield is allowed, but only on accounts with 'material activity' (a payment, a trade). No idle yield. No automatic compounding on parked stables. Both sides left unhappy.

Here's what this means for how you actually deploy capital, and why $KAS becomes the cleaner play once the idle-yield path is gated.

The compromise. The bank lobby pushed for no rewards on idle balances. The crypto side pushed for unrestricted yield. The middle landed at: yield is fine, but the account has to show real usage.

On paper, that sounds like a workable compromise. In practice, it kills the cleanest carry-trade setup we had: park stables on a regulated exchange, earn 4-5% on the float, withdraw when you want to deploy.

That trade required idle yield. Activity-gated yield doesn't replicate it. You'd have to manufacture trades to keep the account 'material', and the cost of those trades will eat the yield in most cases.

Three implications.

First, the compounding-stables crowd has to find a new home. Some of that capital goes to higher-yield DeFi (which carries protocol risk most of those holders won't tolerate). Some goes back into BTC and ETH spot for the optionality. Some goes into PoW alts for the asymmetry.

Second, the idle-yield expectation gets repriced across crypto. If yield on stables requires activity, then 'productive' suddenly looks more attractive on assets that don't pretend to pay yield in the first place. The framing of $KAS as a non-yielding productive asset (deflationary supply curve, hard-capped emission, security budget paid by the protocol itself) becomes the cleaner thesis once the alternative needs a usage gate.

Third, the bear case for the compromise is that it keeps idle stables from becoming a true substitute for treasuries in retail wallets. posts.topic: The Clarity Act yield fight is the whole point
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-21_market-update-polymarket-clarity-meme-rugs.txt
posts.body_style: policy fight + first-person stake + macro takeaway
posts.body:
The Clarity Act is at the Senate floor, and the banking lobby is fighting to gut the one part that actually matters to retail.

Here's the setup. The current text, hammered out by Senators Tillis and Alsobrooks, bans yield that's "economically or functionally equivalent to a bank deposit," but allows yield from "bona fide activities." Translation: USDC, USDT, and the rest can keep paying out yield from real protocol-level activity. Banks can't pretend their checking account is a stablecoin.

The American Bankers Association doesn't love that compromise. They've been writing letters to Senate Banking asking to refine the language, which is bank-lobby code for "narrow it until nothing qualifies." If they win, that 4% you're earning on USDC dies the second this bill passes.

Let me put this in real money. If you've got $10,000 in stablecoins, that 4% is $400 a year. Not life-changing. If you've got $100,000, that's $4,000. Now we're talking. The people who care about this aren't the institutions. They're the retail holders who finally figured out you can park dry powder in a stablecoin and earn more than your savings account pays you.

This is the whole reason regulation matters for crypto. We didn't fight for a decade so the banks could keep stablecoin yield for themselves. We fought so the little guy could earn 4% without asking JPMorgan for permission.

The bill passes Senate Banking 14-9 on May 14. It's now at the full Senate. If the yield language survives, this is the most retail-positive crypto bill in U.S. history. If it gets gutted on the floor, we're back to the same broken setup we've had for years.

I'm watching the markup closely. Anyone who tells you yield doesn't matter is fighting on the bank lobby's side, whether they know it or not.

posts.topic: The AI expansion thesis, anchored by a FedEx story
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/2026-05-21_market-update-polymarket-clarity-meme-rugs.txt
posts.body:
The highest concentration of humanity's best ideas is in a cemetery.

Think about that for a second. Every person who ever lived had ideas, plans, prototypes, sketches, businesses they wanted to start, problems they wanted to solve. Almost all of them never built any of it. They didn't have the time, the capital, the team, or the technical skill. They took the ideas to the grave.

For the first time in history, that gap is closing. One person with AI can ship what used to take a team of ten. The Wall Street consensus reads that as a job displacement story. I read it as the largest economic expansion in modern history about to unlock. The smallest companies are about to do what only the biggest used to.

Here's the other side, because it's real and it's coming faster than people think.

I had a FedEx driver deliver my package of frozen meat to the wrong house. He never told me. My neighbor found it overnight, put it in her freezer, and didn't say anything for a week. By the time I got it back, the meat was thawed, refrozen, and the package was destroyed.

A self-driving truck would have logged the GPS coordinates of the actual drop. A delivery robot would have rung the right doorbell. The "what catalyst?" crowd keeps showing up under my Kaspa posts to ask what's supposed to make the price move. They think the hard fork is the surprise that finally pumps the chart. It's not, and the reason why is the most underappreciated idea in trading.

If the market knows something is coming, it's already in the price.

This is the same mechanic that runs every macro event. When the entire market expects a Fed cut, the day of the cut barely moves the tape. The move happens in the weeks leading in, while everyone repositions. By the time the announcement actually drops, the people who were going to buy have already bought, and the people who were going to sell have already sold. The headline is a non-event.

The Kaspa hard fork is the same setup. The dev team has been openly telegraphing this for months. There's no element of surprise. Anyone who wanted to front-run it has had every chance. So when people say "the hard fork should pump the price" and the chart doesn't cooperate, they're missing that the chart already cooperated quietly, on the way down to here. Maybe $KAS would be at 2 cents right now if the hard fork wasn't on the calendar. Instead it's holding 3.3 cents while $BTC is locked in a 109-day bear flag. That difference is the priced-in.

It cuts the other way too. If the market knows the fork is coming and the price action is flat, a "sell the news" dump after the fork is also baked in. The selling happens during the climb, not after the headline. So when nothing dramatic happens on fork day, that doesn't mean the catalyst failed. It means it already did its job.

This is why I don't trade on calendar dates. I accumulate into boredom. The interesting moves on $KAS won't come from the fork; they'll come from the spot demand wave that hits when retail decides crypto is back. By the time the headline is loud enough for retail to feel it, the bag is built.

There is a name printed inside the Ethereum whitepaper that almost nobody in crypto can pronounce.

It belongs to the man who then went and built Kaspa. Let me put the receipts on the table.

His name is Yonatan Sompolinsky. In 2013, while he was still a student at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, he and his advisor Aviv Zohar published a paper called Secure High-Rate Transaction Processing in Bitcoin. The idea inside it is GHOST, short for Greedy Heaviest Observed Sub-Tree.

Here is the careful part, because the truth is stronger than the hype. Ethereum's whitepaper cites that exact paper, and early Ethereum shipped a simplified version of the idea as the uncle reward. Not "Ethereum runs on his tech." Cited, and adapted. That alone is a fingerprint on the second biggest network in crypto.

He did not stop there. In 2016 came SPECTRE with Zohar and Yoad Lewenberg, turning a single chain into a web of blocks. Then GHOSTDAG, the consensus that keeps every honestly created block and still lays them all down in one agreed order. Bitcoin keeps one block and burns the rest. GHOSTDAG keeps them all. In 2022 he co-authored DAGKnight with Michael Sutton, a consensus that adapts to the network instead of hard-coding its limits.

Then the part that separates him from a thousand brilliant whitepapers that never shipped. In 2021 he launched Kaspa as a live proof of work chain running GHOSTDAG. No premine. No ICO. No presale. No insider allocation. A founder who could have minted himself a fortune chose the credibly neutral way.

No Lambo posts. No countdown to the moon. A quiet academic who published the papers other founders quote.

posts.topic: The Japanese carry trade: capital flight draining liquidity from US markets and crypto
posts.source_transcript: video-creation/longform-edited/media/carry-trade/renders/carry-trade-FINAL.mp4
posts.body:
Japan spent thirty years handing the world free money. That era is ending, and almost nobody is pricing in what happens next.

Here is the part most people miss.

For decades Japan kept interest rates at basically zero. So two very different kinds of money left the country chasing a better return somewhere else. Real money: Japan's own pension funds, life insurers and banks bought foreign bonds and foreign stocks because home paid nothing. Borrowed money: speculators borrowed yen at near zero, converted it, and levered into risk assets, stocks and crypto included.

Both only work while two things stay true. Japan keeps paying nothing, and the yen stays weak. Neither is true anymore.

Japanese bond yields just hit their highest levels since the 1990s. Holding a Japanese bond pays a real return again, and the math that justified sending trillions abroad starts to break. The money is already responding: March 2026 saw the largest monthly inflow ever into Japanese government bond funds, and Japan, the single largest foreign holder of US debt at over a trillion dollars, has started selling.

That drains liquidity out of US markets and crypto at the same time.

Here is the twist for crypto. Japanese pension funds do not hold Bitcoin; their exposure is bonds and stocks. So crypto's risk is indirect through the slow liquidity drain, plus a direct hit if the leveraged side ever squeezes the way it did in August 2024, when $BTC fell from 64K to under 50K in about 48 hours.

If that combination lands while crypto is already soft, it does not start a new crash. It extends the one already underway.

So which is it: are we early in an AI driven expansion that overpowers all of this, or is the carry unwind the risk nobody is watching?

Drop your take below, and subscribe if you want to be early on the setups before they are obvious.

posts.body:
There is exactly one bullish catalyst on the crypto calendar between now and October, and almost nobody is watching the clock on it.

It is not a Fed meeting. It is not an ETF. It is a bill that has been sitting on a Senate calendar since May, and it has about three weeks to live.

The Clarity Act cleared Senate Banking 15 to 9 on May 14th. Since then, nothing. No floor vote scheduled. A merged text that was supposed to drop in mid July still has not landed. August 7th is the last day before the Senate leaves for recess.

Why does that one date matter so much?

Because Clarity is exactly what the name says. Every institution sitting on the sidelines is not sitting there because they hate crypto. They are sitting there because nobody can tell them what they are allowed to do. Give them clear legislation and a large amount of that money finally has permission to move. That is the catalyst this bear market has been starving for.

Now here is the part that should worry you.

What is holding it up is not crypto policy at all. Democrats want an ethics provision that stops public officials from profiting off crypto they sponsor or endorse, and the reason they want it is that Trump's own annual disclosure showed more than 1.4 billion dollars in crypto income last year. Around 635 million in Celebration Coins royalties. Around 527 million from World Liberty Financial token sales. The White House will not swallow the provision. The Democrats will not drop it. The bill needs 60 votes, which means it needs at least seven of them.

In mid July those talks collapsed and a group of Senate Democrats came out publicly calling the bill corrupt. Prediction markets that had this around 70 percent dropped into the low 40s.

So it is a tug of war, and the rope is our summer.

If it passes, that is the bullish catalyst, and everybody who checked out until October misses the front of the move.

If it does not pass before August 7th, the calendar gets ugly fast. Recess, then September, then campaign season, and the realistic next window is 2027.

I am still leaning bullish, because I do not think this market needs a perfect outcome to run. Bitcoin has been refusing to break down through months of genuinely bad news, and that tells you who is left holding it. But this is the one date I would actually put on the wall.

Three weeks. That is the whole setup.

posts.topic: The bottom is being front-run: September 2025 proved it and October cannot be the low
posts.source_transcript: video-creation/livestream-repurpose/transcripts/October-pumps LOW BPS VERTICAL/October-pumps LOW BPS VERTICAL_plain.txt
posts.body_style: pattern-break with a verified receipt, then the mechanical argument
posts.body:
Everyone knows September is red in a post-halving year.

So last year, everyone sold in August instead.

Here is what that did to the chart: August 2025 closed down 6.5%. September 2025 closed UP 5.16%, the third best September on record.

Read that again. The most reliably red month in the entire post-halving playbook turned green, and it turned green precisely BECAUSE everybody knew it was supposed to be red.

That is front-running. It is not a conspiracy and it is not complicated. When a pattern becomes common knowledge, the crowd steps in front of it, and the crowd's own footsteps move the thing they were trying to predict.

Which brings us to right now.

The entire four-year cycle crowd has circled October. October is the bottom, October is when you buy, October is when the pain ends. They have said it on every podcast and in every thread for six months.

Think about what that means mechanically. If millions of people have all agreed to buy in October, October is not allowed to be red. Their own buying is what turns those candles green. A bottom is the reddest month on the chart; it cannot also be the month everyone shows up with cash. So the one thing October almost certainly is NOT is the low.

And it goes a step further. The people who are not four-year cycle believers know all of this too. They know the October crowd is coming. So they do their buying before the crowd arrives, which means late August and September. Which pulls the whole move earlier again.

That is why I think the bottom is either already behind us or it is weeks away in August, not months away in October.

I am not going to pretend there is zero chance of a new low. If enough medium sized bearish things land at once, fresh tariffs on 60 countries, a Bank of Japan hike, a Clarity Act that dies on the Senate calendar, sure, we can print a lower low. But if that happens it happens in August, while the crowd is still standing around waiting for a month their own FOMO already ruined.

And when they finally do show up in October, they are not going to be calm about it. They are going to watch green candle after green candle, realize the bottom never came, and buy anyway. Overwhelmed with FOMO to the point where somebody is scheduling an appointment with a psychiatrist.

So here is what I want to know from you.

Where does the real bottom actually print: is it already behind us, is it August, or do you still think October delivers?

Every single time, liquidity goes where the fun is first, and the utility arrives later, on top of rails that speculation already paid to build.

So when somebody tells you memes are a distraction from real adoption, look at where the volume actually is. The memes ARE the adoption event. They are what gets millions of casual users to make their first onchain transaction, and once those wallets exist they do not disappear when the meta rotates.

posts.topic: The October bottom is a Mandela effect
posts.source_transcript: transcripts/october-bottom LOW BPS VERTICAL_plain.txt
posts.body:
Everybody remembers 1929 and 1987. Almost nobody remembers the other 97 years.

That one asymmetry created the most feared month in markets, and right now it is quietly setting up the biggest head-fake in crypto.

Here is what October actually looks like in the data since 1927:

- Median return: +1.3%
- 62% of Octobers closed GREEN
- Ranked 6th worst of 12 months, dead middle of the pack
- Volatility: about 36% above the monthly average

So October is not a crash month. It is a volatile month that usually closes positive. Two events spread across 90 years is not a pattern, it is an outlier. September actually carries the weakest record on the calendar, and November and December are among the strongest.

Now map that onto crypto. This cycle is the FIRST time the crypto market has ever carried a mainstream prediction of an October bottom. We have literally never had one before. And the moment 90% of the market believes the bottom lands in October, the trade breaks itself: everybody and their grandma plans to buy back in October, the people who know that plan to buy in September, and the people who know THAT are buying now.

A bottom is the point of maximum fear and minimum demand. You cannot pre-schedule maximum fear for a month when everyone has cash ready and a buy order planned. Their own demand is the reason the real low prints early.

My honest odds: 50% the bottom is already behind us. 40% it prints in the next 30 days, way before October. 10% everything else.

The four-year cycle zombies are running the same playbook one more time. The market has a habit of punishing whatever 90% of participants agree on.

So call it: when does this bottom actually print?

Michael Saylor's favorite Bitcoin stat is that it has traded above its 200-week SMA about 92% of the time, by his own math. It is the line his whole thesis leans on. Here is the part that does not make the highlight reel: Bitcoin already lost that line this year, and it is sitting right back on it today.

Late June, Bitcoin closed a week at $59,486 with the 200-week SMA at $62,443. That was its first weekly close beneath that line since the 2022-23 bear market. It clawed back above, and everybody moved on.

The problem is that the average keeps climbing, about $200 every single week, because the sub $20,000 weeks from late 2022 keep rolling out the back of the four year window. It was $62,443 in June. It is near $64,000 now. Bitcoin is around $63,600, which puts it a hair under the line as I write this: it closed above the average last week and has slipped back beneath it since. You do not need a crash to lose this line. You just need another week of nothing, because the line is the thing that is moving.

Now stack what is sitting on top of that.

Supply. MARA sold 23,093 Bitcoin in the first half of this year at an average price of $70,631. That is $1.63 billion of coins moving out of a miner's treasury and back into the market. Their stack went from 53,822 down to 35,577, and only 26,307 of what is left is unrestricted; the rest is loaned out or pledged as collateral.

Jobs. July had 33,429 announced layoffs, a two year low, and hiring plans were the strongest for any July since 2022. Sounds great. Payrolls still printed negative 23,000 against 80,000 expected, with May and June revised down a combined 103,000. Nobody is firing. Nobody is hiring. The whole thing froze in place.

Inflation. CPI came in exactly in line this morning, 3.4% headline and 2.5% core, easing from 3.5% in June. No relief and no shock, which means the week gets decided by PPI on Thursday and retail sales on Friday.

And on the fun side of the market, only 37% of traders across the Robinhood chain's top 50 tokens are in profit. Everybody is spreading the same money across twenty tickets instead of five, so every pump lands smaller than the last one.

Any one of these on its own is noise. Stacked together, they are why I am building dry powder instead of chasing green candles.

Then Trump says he will declare the Strait of Hormuz a United States territory. To actually hold that water you need boots on the ground. That is the worst wrench that could get thrown into this machine.

Every previous bear checked three boxes: price went below the previous cycle high, price went at or below the 200-week SMA, and price tagged the 0.786. This cycle we have checked two of the three. Meanwhile the person selling every local pump and buying the dip back finishes the same move with double, triple, quadruple the bag.

Here is how it compounds. When something runs, I take profits on the way up and rotate the dry powder into the other plays I am already tracking. 200 here, 100 there, 300 somewhere else. So the next time one of them goes parabolic, I am not 350x-ing $80, I am 350x-ing $500. The wins get bigger because the last win paid for them.

I sold into the top and bought back lower, so the bag is bigger now than it was during the 94x.

The catch is you cannot run this on vibes. I did it in spreadsheets until the start of last year and it nearly drove me insane, so I built software that tracks every wallet, every entry, every partial. That is what my community uses.

posts.body:
Bitcoin came 300 dollars short of the line that ends bear markets, and got thrown straight back under 76K.

300 dollars. That is the whole story of this week.

The 50-week SMA sits at 81,455. We tagged it minus a rounding error, got rejected, and by the next day we were printing 76 thousand handles with longs liquidated on the way down. We have been under that line since November of 2025, and it is not a moving average people draw for content: in completed bear markets, 11 of the last 13 reclaims of the 50-week on a weekly close meant the low was already in.

We just failed it by 300 dollars.

Now put the macro next to it. Chicago PMI came in at 47.1 against 57.9 expected, a swing of more than ten points off last month's 57.6. The Richmond Fed manufacturing print missed too. Housing keeps printing badly. And after Warsh spoke, the September Fed meeting is no longer a hold; it is a coin flip on a rate HIKE. We do not like hikes here.

So September gets its leg down. I think that is close to unavoidable, and I do not think it makes a new bottom, because a new bottom needs several bad things happening at the same time, not one bad PMI and a hawkish chair. Easy to say 70K. Easy to say 65K. Neither of those is a new cycle low.

Then October.

Here is what almost nobody gets right about October. It is not the bullish month. I pulled the stock market data for a presentation a few weeks back and October averages out to the middle of the pack, dead center of all twelve months. What it actually is, is the most volatile month of the year, which is the whole reason the famous crashes seem to live there. Not bearish. Swingy.

And swings are two directional.

My read is that it is going to be very hard to print a red October this year, whatever the news does. If things pump, sentiment buys it. If something breaks and we dump, everybody who missed the entire move off the lows finally gets their price. Either way the bid shows up, and red candles do not travel far when the whole market underneath them is waiting to get filled.

That is why I am not trying to time the exact bottom of September. I am trying to be positioned before October, not during it.

So where are you: does Bitcoin reclaim that 50-week line before November, or do we lose 76K first?

posts.body:
Tendies got listed on Crypto.com and printed a brand new all time high the same day. Around 37 million at the top, up 70 percent before it started giving some back.

None of my alerts fired on it. I never hooked Tendies into the system, so there was nothing to fire. That gets fixed tonight.

But here is the part that should bother you more than the alert did.

The same week, a coin called Chump got its listings too. Not a product. Not a team you have heard of. A coin called Chump.

Chump launched on July 31st at a market cap of about 2,230 dollars. It just printed a fresh all time high and it is sitting near 37 million. That is better than a 16,000x in about a month.

So what changed in that month? Not the product, because there isn't one. CoinMarketCap on August 21st. LBank on August 29th. A brand new all time high today. Listings. That is the entire delta.

This is the thing I keep saying and people keep arguing with me about. On this chain the listing is not a milestone that follows the value. The listing IS the value. Insiders plus funding plus a centralized exchange equals a nine figure ambition on a coin whose whole concept is a rhyme with Trump.

Now the other side of it, because this cuts both ways and it will cut you.

Longbow built a real looking website at longbow.cash, a real looking company, an X profile with just enough history to survive a glance. They got their leg up. Then they rugged everybody.

A month later the same dev is back at longbow.credit. Same logo. Different color. It is listed on Ourbit and it is pumping again right now.

That is the pattern, and it is not rare. Fake company, fake history, sometimes a real exchange listing, one leg up, gone. A centralized exchange listing does not prove a project is safe. It proves somebody had the money and the contacts to buy one.

So use listings as the catalyst, never as the diligence. Check whether the X button on the profile goes to an actual account instead of a single post. Check whether they publish content or just publish promises. And check the market cap against the candles before you size in, because DexScreener has been serving stale numbers this week and it will hand you an entry that does not exist.

Would you buy a coin called Chump at 37 million, or is that exactly where you draw the line?

Third objection: no big exchange listing. I have said this for two years and I will say it again. There was no premine to fund a listing. The exclusion is the receipt of the fair launch, not a defect in it. You do not get both: the clean launch and the war chest that buys shelf space.

So what is left? Price. It has not moved yet. That is the whole bear case now, and it is a chart complaint dressed up as analysis.

Here is the part I actually care about. When I put the question to my own community, one in ten went out of their way to say it never gets its moment. Not later. Never. Apathy does not vote. That is a fight, and the fight around this thing is the loudest it has been since I put most of my money in at 11 cents. posts.topic: The Robinhood chain meme mechanic that airdrops real tokenized stocks
posts.source_transcript: video-creation/livestream-repurpose/transcripts/biggest bullrun LOW BPS VERTICAL/biggest bullrun LOW BPS VERTICAL_plain.txt
posts.body_style: mechanic explainer with an honest risk half
posts.body:
A meme coin just paid me in real stock.

Not a promise of revenue share. Not points. Actual tokenized shares, airdropped into the wallet, for doing nothing except holding.

Here is the mechanic, because it is the most interesting thing happening on the Robinhood chain right now and most people are still arguing about which dog is funnier. You hold the token. Every trade pays a small fee. That fee is not going to a team wallet, it is used to buy a basket of tokenized US stocks. Those stocks are then distributed to holders. The INDEX token runs a 3% trade tax and pushes stock tokens out to holders every 15 minutes. Vlad Tenev said the quiet part in public: on Robinhood chain, if you hold a meme coin, you just get stock tokens airdropped to you.

Sit with that for a second. The entire complaint about meme coins, for years, has been that there is nothing underneath them. You buy a picture, you hope somebody buys the picture from you higher. That is the whole trade. This flips it. The picture buys assets and hands them to you while you wait.

Boomer is the cleanest version of the idea I have seen so far. People buy it, people sell it, the fees generated go into a basket of stocks, and the basket gets distributed to the people holding. Own things that pay you. That is not a slogan somebody wrote for a pitch deck, it is literally what the contract does.

Now the part I am not going to skip, because I am not here to sell you a fairy tale. The stock leg does not make the token safe. The same week this mechanic went mainstream, I watched a project paired to a streaming brand ship a site that could not even load a movie, and a chain outage stop block production while everybody was trying to trade. A yield mechanic on top of a broken product is still a broken product, and a chain that stops producing blocks is a chain you cannot sell into. Size accordingly.

But directionally, this is the first meme mechanic I have seen that gives the holder something other than hope. If it works, every chain copies it within a quarter, and the memes that do not pay you start looking very old very fast.

So here is my question for the comments: if a meme coin paid you in real tokenized stock, would you actually hold it longer, or would you still sell the first green candle? Be honest.

First, the price. A 25% day, 32% on the week, and a market cap that crossed a billion dollars for the first time in a long time. This whole bear market the only good news in Kaspa land was the dip letting people buy cheaper. Then the chart woke up.

Second, the delisting. Coinbase pulled nine perpetual futures contracts at 13:00 UTC on September 3: Kaspa was on the list next to Popcat and Brett. Spot trading was untouched. And here is the part that matters: the price ran INTO the delisting, not away from it. Whatever was leaning on that perps market was not the thing holding Kaspa up. No premine means no war chest to buy a listing; the exclusion is the receipt of the fair launch, and a derivatives desk dropping the exposure changes nothing about that.

Third, the attention. Two Bitwise executives, including the CIO, plus BitGo, Gemini and Ivan on Tech all publicly engaged Kaspa in the same week. Not a listing, not a product, and I am not going to invent one. But for two years the objection was "nobody knows what it is," and now the people who decide what Wall Street looks at are saying the name out loud. That gives the folks who dropped out a reason to look twice.

Now the math, because there is an influencer out there saying Kaspa never gets past 10 cents again. 28.7 billion max supply, 96.5% of it already mined, no premine, nobody handed a bag at zero. A $3 Kaspa is an $86 billion market cap. In a crypto market heading for tens of trillions, an $86 billion proof of work layer one is not a fantasy, it is a mid-table outcome. posts.body_style: macro calendar breakdown: Fed reflex under Warsh, Clarity odds, the bear stack, the October zombie read, Kaspa and BTC at the 50-week SMA
posts.body:
This week decides if the whole market goes flying, and almost nobody is pricing the version where it does.

Look at the calendar. September 15: the Senate holds a cloture vote on the Clarity Act. September 16: Warsh's Fed decides on rates. September 18: the Bank of Japan decides, with a hike to 1.25% expected. All of that inside five days, and the crowd has already decided how it ends.

Start with the Fed. A 25 bps hike is about 85% priced in, and since 2007 the Fed has almost always done what the market priced this strongly. Here is the catch: that reflex was learned under Powell, and Powell is gone. Core CPI just printed 2.4% year over year, the lowest since March 2021. Headline CPI is 3.4%, and gasoline alone was over a third of the monthly increase. Warsh has said out loud that he reads through energy. So everyone is pricing Warsh like he is Powell, and if he looks at core at 2.4% and holds, everything positioned for a hike has to reprice at once. Bitcoin first.

Then the Clarity Act. Cloture needs 60 votes and Republicans hold 53, so it needs seven crossovers, and a bloc of Democrats plus the banks are pushing back. Polymarket has passage in 2026 at 16%, down from 82% in February. Two weeks ago I did not think it would even get a vote, so the fact that it is on the floor at all is progress. If it passes, that is the biggest bullish catalyst on the board.

Now the bear stack, because it is real. AI stocks dumped on September 14 after Amodei, Altman and Musk spent the weekend asking the industry to slow down, and the whole stock market has been riding the AI trade. Add a Bank of Japan hike and you get the four-year cycle zombies screaming for a new bottom. They want it in October, because the cycle says so. My read: a September dip does not take Bitcoin anywhere near the $57.7K July low, and the zombies never get their October bottom, because everyone piling back in around October 1 is exactly what turns October green.

And the chart already gave a preview. $KAS ran 33% in a month and poked above its 50-week SMA when that looked close to impossible. Bitcoin has been sitting on its own 50-week SMA for weeks. A hold plus a Clarity pass and it clears the line, and the bull market is on. Even one of the two is enough.

Never financial advice. Never.

posts.source_transcript: video-creation/livestream-repurpose/transcripts/pieverse LOW BPS VERTICAL/pieverse LOW BPS VERTICAL_plain.txt
posts.body_style: stat-stack-and-conclusion: the weekly close and the 50-week SMA, Galaxy's 11 of 13, Cowen's admission and his prior call, the zombies' sell-and-buy-back transfer of wealth, Mike's two-close rule, the year-five / mid-cycle-top thesis with the Bitwise quote, the black-swan caveat
posts.body:
Bitcoin just did something it had not done in 45 weeks, and the king of the four-year cycle zombies posted 'I was wrong' the next day.

The weekly candle closed at $81,159 on September 20. That is above the 50-week SMA (about $78,800) for the first time since November 9, 2025. Forty-five weeks below the line, and the line is reclaimed. Bitcoin is trading around $85K as I write this.

Galaxy Research went back and checked every time Bitcoin reclaimed the 50-week after a bear-market breakdown: 13 comparable cases. In 11 of the 13, no new cycle low followed.

Then Benjamin Cowen, the king of the four-year cycle zombies, posted: 'I was wrong. Not going to make excuses. I deserve to be dunked on.' On September 8 he had 65% odds on the cycle low still being ahead of us, October as the window, $44K in the downside scenarios. Smart guy, honorable admission, and the funny part is that back in 2020 he believed in lengthening cycles before he joined the four-year camp and became its king. The cycle was the problem, not him.

Here is what the zombies did. They sold from October through March because the four-year cycle told them a new bottom was coming in October 2026. The actual low printed at $58K on June 30. Now they are waking up early, realizing the bottom may already be in, and buying back higher than they sold. That is a transfer of wealth, and it goes to the people who never left. They are going to pump our bags.

My rule: two consecutive weekly closes above the 50-week SMA and the bull market is official. One down, one to go.

And I do not think this is a four-year cycle at all. I count this as year five of the current cycle. The 2025 top never broke above the average power law the way every previous mid-cycle top did, which tells me it was a mid-cycle top, not the cycle top. Bitwise's CIO told CNBC this week the crypto winter is over and this could be the strongest and longest bull market in crypto's history. I agree: multiple all-time highs, possibly one every year, for reasons that have nothing to do with a halving.

What would it take for a new bottom now? Something catastrophically bad, a real black swan. Short of that, the zombies buying back in is the fuel.

So call it in the comments: is the bear market over, or is this the head fake the zombies say it is? And if it is over, where do the zombies finally buy back in: $90K, $100K, or higher?

For a year, every other market did well while crypto bled. This week the script started cracking on the other side, and I think the whole thing flips.

Here is the read, and why the four-year cycle zombies are the reason Bitcoin is not being allowed to fall.

The flows first. Spot Bitcoin ETFs logged nine straight days of inflows through Sept 29, about $3.1B, with no sign of sell pressure. Bitcoin ($BTC) put in a weekly close above its May high, the level Benjamin Cowen did not think would get taken out; his own words this week were that he 'clearly got wrong' that break. It keeps tapping that level, trying to go down, and it will not.

Now the cracks everywhere else. The 30-year Treasury yield hit 5.62%, the highest since 2002. Consumer confidence dropped to 81.9, the lowest reading since 2014. JOLTS printed 7.08M job openings against 7.23M expected, a five-month low. Stocks sold off intraday and closed lower. Bond market, stock market, housing: every one of them is showing cracks at the same time.

Why crypto flips. Think about what a weak job market does: it takes a rate hike off the table. And think about who is buying Bitcoin right now. The four-year cycle zombies sold the whole way down last November, pushing Bitcoin under the 50-week SMA, because their script said bear market. Now their script says October bottom, so they are front-running it: they already pushed Bitcoin back above the 50-week SMA and above the May high. If crypto dips, they buy more. Their own demand is why the candles are not allowed to go far.

So the picture I see for Q4: metals, bonds, stocks and energy struggling, and crypto running, because hordes of zombies are buying back in. That is the exact opposite of the past year, and it is why the meme charts that look dead right now are the ones I am holding for the flood.

Jobs beat. Inflation cooled. GDP got revised up. All on the same day, and the odds of a Fed rate hike on Oct 28 fell off a cliff.

Here is why I told my group I do not know if we could ask for anything better, and what it sets up for October.

The data, all from Sept 30:

1. Jobs. ADP private payrolls came in at +90K against 73K expected, more than double the prior month's 38K.

2. Inflation. PCE, the Fed's preferred inflation gauge, printed 3.4% year over year against 3.7% expected, and 0.3% on the month against 0.4%. Core came in under forecast too. One more reading that says inflation is cooling.

3. Growth. The final read on Q2 GDP came in at 2.2% against 1.5% expected.

Employment, inflation, GDP: every one of them better than expected on the same day.

What it did to the Fed. A week ago the market was pricing about a 70% chance of another rate hike on Oct 28. After this data, the odds of NO hike jumped to about 65%, from a coin flip the day before. We need more readings like this and we will be absolutely flying.

Now put crypto on top of that. For the past year every other market did well while crypto sat in a bear market. The scenario I like even more than crypto running alone is everything doing well AND crypto doing well, because that means more money flows into crypto.

And the chart agrees. Bitcoin ($BTC) broke above its May high, and that old resistance is now acting as support: it keeps tapping it on the daily candles and so far it will not go below. Bitcoin dominance is under 60% while the chart of everything outside the top 10 keeps climbing. Benjamin Cowen posted that he 'clearly got wrong' the break above the May high.

That is the part the four-year cycle zombies never see coming. They all planned to buy an October bottom, so their own demand turns October green, and in my read the real low is already behind us. For what it is worth, Bitcoin has closed October higher in 10 of the last 15 years.

Now the comp. Zcash ($ZEC) is sitting in the top 10 this week at about a $24B market cap, up about 66% on the month. Somebody asked me what I think about Zcash. It is another proof-of-work coin you can make money on, but I am not DCAing into it. Optional privacy is a feature, and in my view a feature like that can be built on top of Kaspa.

But look at what that number tells you. The market is paying about $24B for a proof-of-work coin RIGHT NOW. Kaspa at $1 is a $27.7B coin. We are not talking about some fantasy valuation; we are talking about a market cap the market is already handing to a PoW coin this week.

And Kaspa is not standing still. It runs 10 blocks per second on proof of work. The first vProg (a verifiable program: real off-chain execution with zero-knowledge settlement on the L1) went live on testnet in September. I put out a video on vProgs and it pulled 3,600 views in a single day, so people are paying attention.

Fair launch, almost fully mined, 10 blocks per second, and programmability on the way. That is why I say $1.

posts.body:
Bitcoin tagged $87K on the Oct 2 jobs report and gave the whole move back within hours. About $434M got liquidated in 24 hours, and roughly three quarters of it was longs.

That is a bull trap on the daily chart. Here is the question I keep coming back to: what if the whole market is setting one up for October?

Look at how fast the mood flipped. A few weeks ago the four-year cycle zombies were all waiting for an October bottom. That talk is gone. Now CNBC is telling its audience Bitcoin is setting up for a big fourth quarter, and the talking points are real:

1. Citi raised its price target on Strategy to $240 from $136, and its 12-month Bitcoin forecast to $113K from $82K.

2. There have only been three red Octobers since 2013: 2014, 2018 and 2025.

3. CryptoQuant shows whale stablecoin inflows to Binance up about 40% in a month, to $30.5B.

4. Jobs came in at 29K against about 90K expected, and prediction markets now price about an 82% chance the Fed holds rates on Oct 28.

All of that is bullish. And when everybody leans the same way, that is exactly how a trap gets set.

The scenario I am watching. Bitcoin ($BTC) opened October at about $83,555. It runs for another week or two, maybe to $90K, pulls everybody back in, then rolls over and closes the month below that open. That is a red October, the opposite of what everybody is pricing in.

Notice where the money is going too. The total crypto market crossed $3 trillion in late September, but the money is flowing into the top 100. Mid caps, low caps and micro caps are bleeding out.

I am not turning bearish. Bitcoin has two weekly closes above the 50-week SMA and it is above the May high, so for me the bull market is official. The low near $58K this summer was the bottom. We are not going back there, and forget $40K. A red October would be a pullback inside a bull market.

But parabolic? Not yet. ISM Manufacturing PMI printed 54.5 for September. It spent most of three years under 50, broke out in January, and has been grinding sideways above it for nine straight months instead of shooting up. We need that number above 60 before I start talking about a parabolic run.

So bet right now, in the comments: does Bitcoin close October above or below $83,555?
